“Norm” means “how long is this arrow?” Regularization, clipping, and distance-based models all need a length.
L1 norm is the sum of absolute values. |3| + |−4| = 7. It treats each axis separately and likes sparsity.
L2 norm is the usual Euclidean length. √(3² + (−4)²) = 5. It is rotation-friendly and the default for “distance.”
We write ||w||₂ for L2. Gradient clipping often uses this length. “Unit vector” means we divided by the L2 norm so the length is 1.
L1 adds the absolute values. L2 is the ordinary straight-line length.

The closest red and blue training points determine where an SVM puts its separating line. Faraway points matter less.
Move one of those closest points and the boundary may shift; move a distant point and it often stays put.
Two separating lines classify every training point correctly, but one leaves a wider gap to the nearest points. An SVM prefers that wider margin.
A narrow gap can make a tiny measurement change flip the class, while a wider gap offers more room.
A bag with only red balls has entropy 0: the next color is certain.
A bag with half red and half blue balls has higher entropy: the next color is harder to guess.
A node with 10 cats and no dogs has Gini impurity 0 because it is pure.
A node split evenly between cats and dogs has Gini impurity 0.5 for two classes.
A yes/no question divides a mixed basket into one all-apple basket and one all-orange basket. That split gains a lot of information.
A question that leaves both child baskets just as mixed as the parent gains little information.
A tree memorizes a branch for one unusual training row. Removing that branch may improve predictions on new rows.
Try a shallow and deep tree: the deep one can fit training data better while doing worse on validation data.
From rows A, B, C, D, draw four times with replacement: A, C, A, D is a valid bootstrap sample.
A tree trained on that sample sees A twice and never sees B; another tree receives a different sample.
Three trees trained on different bootstrap samples vote cat, cat, dog. Their bagged classification is cat.
Averaging predictions from several regression trees can reduce the wobble of one tree.
The first small tree misses several hard examples. The next tree pays more attention to those mistakes.
Many modest trees added in sequence can correct one another, but too many can overfit without a stopping rule.
Shuffle the “study hours” column. If validation accuracy drops from 90% to 70%, that feature was useful to this model.
Two strongly correlated columns can share credit, so a low importance score does not always mean a feature is irrelevant.
On a chosen output scale, a baseline score of 0.4 plus a +0.2 age contribution and a −0.1 income contribution gives 0.5.
For one prediction, a SHAP waterfall shows which features push the model output up and which push it down.
Ordered sizes small, medium, large can be encoded 0, 1, 2 when that order is meaningful.
Encoding red, blue, green as 0, 1, 2 may invent a false order; one-hot encoding is often safer for unordered colors.
If exam scores have mean 50 and standard deviation 10, a score of 70 becomes z = (70 − 50)/10 = 2.
Fit mean and standard deviation on training rows, then use those same numbers for validation and test rows.
For a training range of 10 to 30, the value 20 becomes (20 − 10)/(30 − 10) = 0.5.
A later value of 40 becomes 1.5 with the same fitted scaler; min-max scaling does not guarantee future values stay below 1.
From (0, 0) to (3, 4), straight-line Euclidean distance is 5.
A k-NN classifier can compare that distance from a new point to every training point and use the nearest ones.
From (0, 0) to (3, 4), moving three blocks east and four north gives Manhattan distance 7.
On a city grid with no diagonal streets, block distance describes the route more naturally than straight-line distance.
Slide a small filter across an image. At each position, multiply nearby pixels by filter weights and add them to produce one output value.
The same edge-detecting filter can find a vertical border near the left or right side of a photo.
A 3×3 blur kernel averages nearby pixels so isolated noise becomes less visible.
An edge kernel gives opposite signs to pixels on either side of a border, making that border stand out.
With stride 1, a filter moves one pixel at a time and checks many overlapping patches.
With stride 2, it jumps two pixels each move, producing a smaller feature map.
A 3×3 filter on a 3×3 image produces one value without padding.
Add a one-pixel border of zeros and the same filter can also be centered on edge pixels, producing a 3×3 output at stride 1.
Max pooling on values [1, 4; 2, 3] keeps 4 as the summary of that 2×2 region.
Average pooling on the same region returns 2.5; it keeps overall level rather than the strongest signal.
An edge filter produces a map with bright values where the photo has a strong border.
A later CNN layer can combine edge maps into a pattern that responds to a corner or eye.
While reading “the dog ran,” an RNN carries information from “dog” into the step for “ran.”
In a long sentence, early information may fade after many recurrent steps; gated models help retain it.
An LSTM can keep the word “not” in memory until it reaches “good,” changing the meaning of the phrase.
Its gates decide what to keep, what to forget, and what part of memory to expose at each step.
In “The dog chased the ball because it rolled,” the token “it” can attend strongly to “ball.”
Each token can inspect other tokens in the same sequence rather than depending only on the immediately previous word.
For the word “it,” the query asks what earlier word it refers to; keys from “dog” and “ball” compete for attention.
If “ball” gets the stronger match, its value contributes more to the new representation of “it.”
“Dog bites man” and “Man bites dog” contain the same words; positions help a Transformer tell the sentences apart.
Position information lets attention distinguish a word at the start of a sentence from the same word near the end.
Start with an image model trained on many everyday photos, then reuse its visual features for a smaller plant-leaf dataset.
A pretrained language encoder can supply useful text representations before you train a task-specific classifier.
Load a pretrained image model, replace its last classifier, and train on your own flower labels.
After the new head works, unfreeze some earlier layers with a small learning rate so the features adapt gently.
For y = 2x + 1, weight 2 says each extra study hour adds two predicted points; bias 1 is the prediction at zero hours.
Changing a weight alters how strongly an input matters. Changing the bias shifts every prediction up or down.
With 100 training rows and batch size 20, one epoch contains five update steps.
A smaller batch gives noisier updates but needs less memory; a larger batch averages more examples per update.
In translation, attention can connect “bank” with nearby words about money or a river before choosing a meaning.
A Transformer handles many tokens in parallel while attention mixes information across their positions.
A straight line tries to model a U-shaped relationship. Both training and validation errors stay high.
Adding useful features or a more flexible model may help when the model is too simple to learn the pattern.
The true value is 10 and a model predicts 8. Absolute error is 2; squared error is 4.
For a yes/no label, cross-entropy penalizes a confident wrong probability more than an uncertain wrong one.
With 100 training rows and batch size 25, the model processes four batches per epoch.
One batch might contain rows 1–25; its average gradient is used for one update before the next batch arrives.
Train three tree depths on training data, compare them on validation data, then choose the depth that generalizes best.
Keep a separate test set sealed until the end; repeated tuning on the test set makes it another validation set.
Compare classical predictive models by the assumptions they make and the outputs they produce.
Linear regression with an L2 penalty on coefficient size.
The penalty shrinks large weights to reduce sensitivity to noisy or correlated features.
A house-price model uses many correlated size measurements and ridge keeps their coefficients moderate.
When two sensors carry almost the same signal, ridge spreads influence instead of fitting huge opposing weights.
Scale features before comparing penalty strength across columns.
Linear regression with an L1 penalty that can set some coefficients to zero.
The penalty can perform a form of feature selection while fitting a linear predictor.
A marketing model starts with 100 predictors and lasso leaves only a smaller set with nonzero weights.
A text regression model drops many irrelevant word-count features when their coefficients become zero.
With strongly correlated inputs, the selected feature can change across samples.
Linear regression combining L1 and L2 coefficient penalties.
It mixes sparse feature selection with the stabilizing effect of ridge shrinkage.
A genetics model has many related measurements and uses elastic net to keep a manageable group of predictors.
A sales model tunes both penalties to retain useful correlated signals without huge coefficients.
Both penalty strengths need tuning on validation data.
A classifier that seeks a separating boundary with a wide margin.
Examples nearest the boundary, called support vectors, determine the fitted margin.
A two-class flower dataset is separated by a line positioned as far as possible from nearby flowers.
With a kernel, an SVM can separate curved groups that a straight boundary cannot split.
Feature scaling and kernel settings can strongly affect the boundary.
Predict a number while allowing errors inside a chosen tolerance tube.
The model focuses its fit on points outside an epsilon-wide band around predictions.
A temperature model treats errors within one degree as acceptable and penalizes larger misses.
A kernel SVR fits a curved relation between engine load and fuel use.
The tolerance, regularization, kernel, and feature scale all need care.
Classify using class distributions with a shared covariance estimate.
Its assumptions lead to linear decision boundaries between classes.
A flower classifier estimates each species center and uses a straight boundary between groups.
LDA projects measurements onto directions that separate known classes.
Shared covariance and distribution assumptions can be poor for irregular classes.
Classify using a separate covariance estimate for each class.
Different class spreads allow curved decision boundaries.
Two species have differently shaped measurement clouds, so QDA bends the dividing curve.
A medical classifier allows one diagnosis to vary more than another across measurements.
Separate covariance estimates can be unstable with few examples per class.
Model event counts using a log-linked expected count.
It predicts a nonnegative event rate from input features.
A service predicts the number of support calls per hour from time and staffing levels.
A city estimates crash counts for roads with different traffic volumes and exposure.
Strong overdispersion may require a different count model.
Predict ordered categories while respecting their ranking.
The labels have an order but the distance between neighboring labels is not necessarily equal.
A review model predicts one through five stars without treating the gap as a measured quantity.
A health survey predicts low, medium, or high severity from patient answers.
A method assuming one common effect across thresholds may fit poorly when effects differ.
Fit a flexible nondecreasing relationship between an input and output.
It preserves order while allowing flat sections and nonlinear steps.
A probability calibrator maps larger raw risk scores to probabilities that never decrease.
A dose-response estimate rises or stays flat as dosage increases.
It can overfit small calibration sets and cannot represent a truly decreasing relationship without reversing the input.
Explore unsupervised algorithms for grouping data and simplifying representations.
Partition points into k groups around iteratively updated centers.
Assign each point to a nearby center, then move centers toward assigned points.
A retailer groups customers into three clusters using spending and visit frequency.
A color compressor replaces many image colors with the nearest of eight learned centers.
The chosen k, feature scaling, and starting centers affect the result.
Build nested groups by merging or splitting clusters.
A dendrogram records how groups join at different similarity levels.
A biologist groups species and then cuts the tree to see either broad or narrow families.
A document collection shows closely related articles merging before larger topic groups.
Distance and linkage choices can produce very different trees.
Group dense regions and mark sparse points as noise.
Clusters form from points with enough nearby neighbors rather than a chosen cluster count.
GPS traces reveal two crowded pickup zones while isolated locations become noise.
A moon-shaped dataset stays in two curved clusters that k-means may split poorly.
One distance threshold can struggle when cluster densities differ greatly.
Model data as a weighted combination of Gaussian distributions.
Each point receives probabilities of belonging to the mixture components.
A customer near two segments gets 60% membership in one and 40% in another.
A sensor distribution with two peaks is modeled by two overlapping bell curves.
The assumed Gaussian shapes and number of components may not match real data.
Cluster points using eigenvectors of a similarity graph.
A graph representation can separate shapes that are not compact around a center.
Two intertwined circles become distinct groups when nearby-point connections are analyzed.
A network of users splits into communities based on connection strengths.
The similarity graph and cluster count require choices, and large graphs can be costly.
Move candidate centers toward dense regions of the data.
Repeated local averaging finds peaks of estimated density.
Points in a photo color space move toward common color modes for segmentation.
Store locations settle around several busy geographic centers without setting k first.
Bandwidth determines how many modes appear and can be expensive to tune.
Project data onto orthogonal directions of greatest variance.
A small number of components can summarize much of the data spread.
Twenty correlated sensor readings become two components for a compact chart.
A face dataset is compressed into leading variation directions before another model is trained.
High variance need not mean high predictive value, and scaling changes the result.
Separate observed mixtures into statistically independent source signals.
It looks for hidden components that combine to form the measurements.
Two microphones record overlapping speakers and ICA estimates the separate voices.
Brain-signal analysis separates some artifact components from neural activity.
Independence is an assumption; component scale and ordering are not uniquely identified.
Embed high-dimensional points into a few dimensions while emphasizing local neighbors.
Nearby points in the source space are encouraged to remain nearby in the map.
A researcher plots word embeddings to inspect whether related words form local groups.
An image dataset map reveals neighborhoods of visually similar samples.
Large distances and cluster sizes in a t-SNE chart should not be read as exact global geometry.
Build a low-dimensional embedding from a graph of nearby data points.
It uses neighborhood structure to organize a compact map of complex data.
Thousands of cell measurements become a two-dimensional view for exploration.
A product-embedding map places similar descriptions in nearby regions.
The view depends on neighbors, distance settings, and random seed; visual gaps are not proof of separate classes.
Recognize major deep learning architectures and the data they suit.
A neural network that reuses local filters across spatial inputs.
Shared kernels detect patterns such as edges wherever they occur in an image.
A classifier combines edge and texture features to recognize a cat in a photo.
A medical model scans local image regions before deciding whether a scan contains a lesion.
A CNN still needs representative data and can be sensitive to distribution shift.
Process a sequence by carrying a hidden state from one step to the next.
Earlier sequence information influences later predictions through the evolving state.
A text model reads words in order and predicts the next word from its current hidden state.
A sensor model updates its state each minute to forecast a future reading.
Long sequences can be hard to learn without gating or another architecture.
A recurrent network with gates that control stored and forgotten information.
A cell state helps useful information survive across many sequence steps.
A demand model remembers a weekly pattern while reading daily sales observations.
A language model keeps subject information until it reaches a later verb.
LSTMs can be slower to parallelize across time than attention-based models.
A recurrent layer with gates that manage its hidden state.
Update and reset gates decide how much old sequence information to keep.
A wearable-sensor model uses a GRU to combine measurements across recent seconds.
A small translation model remembers earlier words without an LSTM cell state.
A simpler gate design is not automatically better; compare on the actual sequence task.
Learn node or graph representations by exchanging information along edges.
A node aggregates messages from connected neighbors over several layers.
A molecule model combines atom features with bond connections to predict a property.
A fraud model links accounts and transactions to spot suspicious neighborhoods.
Poor graph construction or too many layers can blur distinct node information.
Use Transformer attention on image patches or visual tokens.
Patch representations interact through attention to capture image relationships.
An image classifier splits a photograph into patches and predicts its category.
A vision backbone provides patch features for later detection or segmentation.
Patch size, data scale, and compute can strongly affect performance.
A bidirectional Transformer encoder trained with masked-token objectives.
Its contextual representations use words on both sides of a token.
A sentence classifier uses BERT features to label customer feedback sentiment.
A question-answering model selects an answer span from a provided passage.
A base BERT encoder is not a left-to-right text generator by itself.
A decoder-only Transformer trained to predict the next token.
It generates text autoregressively from a prompt and prior output.
A writing assistant continues a paragraph by predicting one token at a time.
A code model proposes the next lines after reading the current function.
Fluent output is not evidence that its factual claims are correct.
An encoder-decoder network with skip connections between matching scales.
Fine spatial details from early layers help a decoder build pixel-level output.
A medical model marks tumor pixels while retaining precise boundaries.
A diffusion model uses a U-Net-like network to estimate image noise at each step.

Encode two inputs with shared weights and compare their representations.

Two signature images are compared to decide whether the same person wrote them.
A product search model compares a query image with candidate item images.
The quality of positive and negative training pairs strongly affects similarity.
Distinguish computer vision tasks by the kind of output they require.

A vehicle model locates wheel centers to estimate orientation.

A driving model estimates how nearby vehicles shift between consecutive frames.
A video editor uses motion fields to create a smoother intermediate frame.

Predict the distance from a camera to scene points.

A robot uses a camera depth map to avoid furniture in a room.
A photo-editing tool separates foreground and background using estimated relative depth.

Generate a higher-resolution image from a lower-resolution input.

An old low-resolution portrait is upscaled for a larger display.

Fill a missing or masked region of an image.

A damaged historical image has a missing corner reconstructed from nearby texture.

Answer a text question using information in an image.

Classify images using candidate text labels without task-specific labeled training.

Choose language and audio tasks by identifying the required output.
Produce a shorter account of a longer text while retaining its main points.

Produce a sequence of text tokens from a prompt or context.

A code assistant continues a function after reading its signature.

A navigation app reads upcoming street directions in a chosen voice.

Assign one or more labels to an audio clip.

A broadly pretrained model that can be adapted to many downstream tasks.

Continue training a pretrained model on labeled input-output examples.

Adjust a model using comparisons between preferred and less-preferred outputs.

The amount of input and generated tokens a model can consider in one run.

A reusable structure for filling task-specific instructions and inputs.

A classification template supplies labels, rules, and a customer message.

Generated content that states unsupported or false information as if it were true.
A fluent answer can be ungrounded in evidence or inconsistent with supplied material.
A chatbot invents a paper title that does not exist.
A document assistant cites a section number that is absent from the uploaded policy.
Check important claims against trusted sources; confidence of wording is not proof.
Connect a model response to relevant evidence, data, or observations.

A support answer quotes the actual return-policy paragraph it used.
A visual assistant points to the chart bar that supports its answer.

Process or produce information across more than one modality.

A model answers a question about an uploaded photo using both image and text input.
A system turns a spoken request into a generated image description.

Name the task before selecting a dataset, model, and evaluation metric.
Suggest items a user may find useful or relevant.

An online store suggests accessories related to a customer’s recent purchases.

Identify observations that differ from expected patterns.

A shop forecasts next week’s daily demand for bread.
A grid operator predicts electricity use for the next 24 hours.

Order candidates by estimated relevance or utility.

A search engine puts the most relevant page first for a query.
A recruiter orders job matches so the best candidates appear early.

Assign any number of applicable labels to one example.

Choose one class from more than two mutually exclusive classes.
One prediction belongs to one of several possible categories.

Choose between two target classes for each example.
A score or probability is converted to one of two decisions.
An email filter marks an incoming message as spam or not spam after scoring its content.

The output is a measured quantity rather than a discrete class.
A model predicts a home price in rupees from property details.
A weather model estimates tomorrow’s high temperature in degrees.

Group examples by similarity without supplied class labels.

One partition used as validation data while the others train the model.

A shopping app learns which products users prefer at the top of results.

Train and evaluate when one target class is much rarer than another.

A medical screen sees far more healthy results than rare conditions.
Evaluate minority-class errors and use appropriate sampling or weights.
Give some training examples more influence on a model update or metric.

A saved snapshot of model weights and often training state.

Read dataset examples progressively without downloading the full dataset first.

Trying to trace a curved road with a ruler: the straight line misses the bend everywhere.
Use this diagnosis when both training and validation performance are poor.
Measures how wrong the model’s predictions are.
A loss function turns a prediction mistake into a number that training can try to reduce.
Different tasks need different scoreboards: squared error for numbers, cross-entropy for class probabilities.
A scoreboard that gives a larger penalty to mistakes the task considers more serious.
Choose a loss that matches the kind of target and error you care about.
A small subset of data used for one update step.
Rather than read the entire dataset before every update, training can process a smaller batch of rows.
The model combines the examples in that batch to estimate one gradient and make one parameter update.
Marking a stack of 25 quizzes, then adjusting the lesson before marking the next stack.
Batching helps training fit in memory and controls how noisy each update is.
Data used to tune and evaluate the model.
The validation set is held out from fitting weights and used to compare settings such as tree depth or learning rate.
After choosing settings, a separate test set gives the final unbiased check. Repeatedly tuning on validation can still overfit it.
A practice exam for choosing a study plan; the final test stays sealed until the end.
Use validation during model selection and early stopping, never as a substitute for a final test set.
