Use these ideas when preparing or monitoring a machine learning dataset.
Fill absent feature values using a rule learned from available data.
Choose a fill value from training data and apply that same rule to new rows.
If five training ages are missing, fill them with the training median age before fitting a model.
When a new record has no age, use the saved median rather than recomputing it from incoming records.
A made-up value can hide why data was missing; consider a missingness indicator too.
Incorrect or inconsistent target labels in a dataset.
A model trained on wrong answers may learn the labeling mistakes instead of the real pattern.
A photo of a cat tagged as dog tells a classifier the wrong answer during training.
Two reviewers give the same medical note different labels, making the target uncertain.
Inspect suspicious labels before assuming more model complexity will fix them.
A change in the input data distribution after a model is deployed.
Compare incoming features with the training population to see whether the world has moved.
A store model trained on winter purchases sees mostly summer products in July.
A camera model trained on daylight photos receives many dim nighttime images later.
A shifted input distribution does not always mean accuracy fell; check labeled outcomes when possible.
A change in the relationship between inputs and the correct target over time.
The same features can begin to imply a different answer, so an old decision rule becomes stale.
A word that once signaled spam becomes common in legitimate email after a product launch.
Fraudsters change tactics, so an old transaction pattern no longer predicts fraud reliably.
Input drift and concept drift are different; concept drift needs outcome evidence to confirm.
Input frequencies change while the rule for targets given inputs stays the same.
The model sees different kinds of cases, even though each kind still obeys the old label rule.
A clinic receives more older patients, but risk at a given age and health profile is unchanged.
A sales model sees more weekend shoppers while the purchase rule within each group stays stable.
Do not assume the target rule is stable without checking; otherwise this may be concept drift.
An input unlike the examples a model learned from.
A familiar-looking confidence score can be unreliable on unfamiliar inputs.
A digit classifier trained on handwritten numbers receives a photo of a street sign.
A plant disease model trained on leaves is asked to classify a picture of a shoe.
High softmax confidence does not prove an unfamiliar input is safe or correctly classified.
Sample each class or group in planned proportions.
Preserving class proportions can make small splits more representative.
A dataset with 10% positive cases keeps roughly 10% positives in both train and test splits.
A survey samples separately from rural and urban groups so neither disappears in the sample.
Stratification alone does not prevent leakage from duplicate people or future records.
Keep all records from one person or entity in the same data split.
Shared identity can leak between train and test even when individual rows are different.
All X-rays from one patient stay together rather than putting one scan in training and another in testing.
All reviews from a single user stay in one split when evaluating a user-level text model.
Choose the grouping unit that will be unseen at deployment, not merely the easiest column.
Train on earlier observations and evaluate on later ones.
Respecting time prevents the model from learning from its own future.
Train a demand forecast on January through June, validate on July, and test on August.
In rolling evaluation, fit on months 1–6, test on 7, then fit on 1–7 and test on 8.
Random shuffling can leak future patterns into training and give an optimistic score.
Create useful inputs from raw data for a predictive model.
A feature should capture a pattern available at prediction time.
Turn a timestamp into hour of day so a traffic model can learn rush-hour effects.
Create purchase count over the last 30 days as an input to a churn model.
A feature computed using future outcomes is leakage, however predictive it looks.
Use these measures to judge predictions on data that was not used for training.
How well predicted probabilities match observed frequencies.
Among cases assigned about 70% probability, roughly 70% should be positive.
Of 100 patients given a 0.8 risk score, about 80 would have the outcome in a well-calibrated model.
A weather model saying 30% rain on many days should see rain on about 30% of those days.
A model can rank cases well while its probabilities remain poorly calibrated.
Mean squared error between predicted probabilities and binary outcomes.
Lower scores mean probabilities are closer to the observed zero-or-one labels.
Predicting 0.8 for an event that occurs gives squared error (0.8 − 1)² = 0.04.
Predicting 0.8 for an event that does not occur gives squared error (0.8 − 0)² = 0.64.
Compare Brier scores on the same task and class balance; the scale depends on the data.
A summary of probability gaps across confidence bins.
Group predictions by confidence and compare each bin with its observed accuracy.
If 100 predictions near 0.8 are correct only 60 times, that bin contributes a 0.2 calibration gap.
A second bin near 0.4 with 40% observed positives contributes almost no gap.
ECE depends on bin choices and can hide local errors; inspect a reliability diagram too.
The fraction of actual negatives correctly rejected.
Specificity is true negatives divided by true negatives plus false positives.
A test correctly clears 90 of 100 healthy people, giving 90% specificity.
If an alert system falsely flags many normal payments, its specificity falls.
High specificity says little about how many positive cases were missed.
The average of recall for the positive and negative classes.
It gives each class equal weight even when one class has far more rows.
A classifier catches 80% of positives and 60% of negatives; balanced accuracy is 70%.
Always predicting the majority class in a two-class problem often gives 50% balanced accuracy.
It summarizes class recall but does not capture probability quality or error costs.
A binary-classification score using all four confusion-matrix cells.
MCC ranges from −1 to 1: perfect disagreement to perfect agreement.
A classifier predicting the same class for everyone has MCC near 0 despite high accuracy on imbalanced data.
A model that gets positives and negatives all right scores MCC = 1.
MCC can be undefined if a denominator is zero; report the confusion matrix alongside it.
Area under the precision–recall curve across thresholds.
It summarizes the trade-off between finding positives and avoiding false alarms.
Two fraud models may have similar accuracy, but the one keeping precision high at high recall has better PR-AUC.
As the threshold falls, recall may rise while precision drops; those points form the PR curve.
PR-AUC changes with positive-class prevalence, so compare on the same evaluation population.
Count a prediction as correct if the true class appears in the top k guesses.
This is useful when several plausible classes can be shown to a person.
A photo model ranks dog first, wolf second, fox third; a wolf image is wrong at top-1 but right at top-3.
A recommendation tool is successful if a relevant item appears among the first five suggestions.
Always state k; top-5 accuracy is usually easier to achieve than top-1.
A range that reflects uncertainty in an estimated result.
Repeated samples produce different estimates; an interval describes that sampling variability.
A test accuracy estimate of 82% might have a 95% interval from 78% to 86%.
Resampling patients can give a range for model recall instead of one fragile number.
A 95% confidence interval is not a 95% probability that a fixed parameter lies in this observed interval.
Choose the probability cutoff used to turn scores into class decisions.
Move the cutoff to trade missed positives against false alarms.
A fraud detector lowered from 0.5 to 0.2 catches more fraud but investigates more legitimate payments.
A screening test may favor high recall, while an expensive intervention may require higher precision.
Choose the cutoff on validation data, then report final performance once on untouched test data.
Use these model families when matching a method to the data and prediction task.
A decision tree with just one split.
One question divides the data into two leaves with their own predictions.
A stump asks whether study hours exceed five, then predicts pass on one side and fail on the other.
Boosting can combine many weak one-split trees into a stronger classifier.
One split is easy to explain but cannot represent several interacting conditions alone.
An ensemble of decision trees trained on resampled rows and random feature subsets.
Different trees vote or average, reducing the instability of one deep tree.
If three trees vote cat, cat, dog, the forest predicts cat.
For house prices, average estimates from many trees to smooth one tree’s noisy prediction.
A forest can fit noise if tuned poorly; evaluate on held-out data.
A tree ensemble that adds extra randomness when choosing split thresholds.
Random candidate splits can make the trees less alike.
One tree tries a random age threshold of 30 while another tries 45 before selecting useful splits.
Average many randomized trees to reduce the variance of a single decision tree.
Extra randomness may raise bias; compare with random forests on validation data.
Build small trees sequentially so each new tree corrects the current model.
Each stage fits a direction that reduces the chosen loss.
A first tree predicts house prices roughly; the next tree learns patterns in its residual errors.
A later tree corrects cases that earlier trees systematically underpredicted.
Too many stages or overly deep trees can overfit; use validation and regularization.
A boosting method that gives more emphasis to examples previous learners got wrong.
Weak learners are combined with weights based on their performance.
After one stump misses several spam messages, the next stump focuses more on those hard cases.
Several modest rules vote together, with stronger rules receiving more say.
Mislabeled outliers can attract too much weight because they remain hard to classify.
A probabilistic classifier that treats features as conditionally independent given a class.
The simplifying independence assumption makes learning fast even with many features.
A spam filter combines evidence from words such as “offer” and “winner” to score spam probability.
A document classifier can use word counts to choose among news topics.
Correlated features violate the assumption; probabilities may need calibration.
Predict from the labels or values of the closest stored training examples.
The choice of distance and k controls what counts as a neighborhood.
If the five nearest flower measurements include four setosa, k-NN predicts setosa.
A new house can be priced by averaging prices of similar nearby houses.
Unscaled features or very high dimensions can make distance misleading.
A probabilistic model over possible functions, with uncertainty for predictions.
A kernel describes which inputs should have similar outputs.
With a few temperature readings, a Gaussian process predicts a smooth curve plus wider uncertainty between readings.
Bayesian optimization can query where a Gaussian process predicts improvement or uncertainty.
Exact training scales poorly with many observations without approximations.
A setting chosen before training rather than learned directly from training examples.
Use validation data to compare settings such as tree depth or learning rate.
The depth limit of a decision tree is a hyperparameter; the chosen split thresholds are learned.
A neural network’s learning rate is chosen by the experimenter while its weights are learned.
Tuning on the test set leaks information and makes the reported score optimistic.
Choose the next expensive experiment using a model of earlier results.
A surrogate model balances promising settings with uncertain unexplored settings.
After testing several learning rates, it suggests one that may improve validation accuracy.
A Gaussian-process surrogate may choose a point with uncertain but potentially high performance.
It helps when evaluations are costly; for a tiny search space, simple search may suffice.
Use these techniques when training large or difficult neural networks.
Estimate the gradient after a look-ahead step in the momentum direction.
Looking ahead can correct an update before it overshoots a valley.
A ball rolling toward a minimum checks the slope where its momentum would take it, then steers sooner.
In an optimizer, the gradient is evaluated at an anticipated parameter position rather than only the current one.
It still needs a suitable learning rate; momentum alone does not prevent divergence.
Scale each parameter update by a moving average of recent squared gradients.
Coordinates with consistently large gradients receive smaller effective steps.
If one weight has gradients near 100 and another near 1, RMSprop reduces the first coordinate’s step.
On a narrow loss valley, adaptive scaling can reduce side-to-side oscillation.
Adaptive scaling does not remove the need to tune a base learning rate.
Adapt each learning rate using accumulated squared gradients.
Frequently updated coordinates shrink their steps over time.
A rare word feature gets relatively larger updates than a frequent word feature.
On sparse text features, per-coordinate step sizes help infrequent features learn.
The accumulated denominator only grows, so learning rates can become too small.
Start training with a small learning rate and raise it gradually.
Gentle early updates help stabilize a model before using its intended step size.
A Transformer increases its learning rate over the first 1,000 updates rather than starting at full speed.
A large batch run warms up over early steps to avoid unstable initial weight changes.
Warmup is a schedule, not a substitute for checking the later learning rate.
Decrease the learning rate along a smooth cosine-shaped schedule.
Steps shrink gradually near the end of a training cycle.
A run starts at 0.01 and smoothly approaches 0.0001 over its planned epochs.
A schedule with restarts raises the learning rate again at the next cycle boundary.
The schedule depends on a chosen cycle length; stopping early changes its effect.
Add gradients from several small batches before one optimizer update.
Several memory-friendly microbatches approximate a larger effective batch.
With microbatch size 8 and four accumulation steps, one update uses gradients from 32 examples.
A GPU unable to fit 64 images at once can process eight images eight times before stepping.
Average or scale gradients correctly, and account for batch-dependent layers.
Use lower-precision arithmetic for suitable operations while retaining needed stability.
Reduced precision can save memory and speed compatible hardware.
A GPU computes many matrix multiplications in 16-bit format while keeping selected accumulations in 32-bit.
A larger batch may fit in memory after switching eligible operations to lower precision.
Small gradients may underflow; use appropriate scaling and check numerical stability.
Save fewer intermediate activations and recompute them during backpropagation.
Trade extra computation for lower training memory use.
A deep network stores outputs only at selected layers and recomputes skipped activations on the backward pass.
A long Transformer sequence may fit in GPU memory after checkpointing several blocks.
Training becomes slower because some forward computations run again.
Keep selected pretrained weights unchanged during a new training task.
Only unfrozen parameters receive optimizer updates.
Freeze an image encoder and train a new classifier head for plant species.
Later unfreeze the last few encoder layers to adapt them to leaf textures.
A fully frozen backbone may not capture a very different target domain.
Arrange training examples from easier to harder according to a plan.
A useful ordering can help a model learn a stable foundation before difficult cases.
A speech model first trains on clean recordings and later includes noisier audio.
A robot practices short routes before attempting longer obstacle courses.
The chosen difficulty order can bias learning; compare against ordinary shuffled training.
Use these terms when designing or evaluating computer vision systems.
The region of input pixels that can influence one feature-map value.
Deeper layers can combine information from a larger part of an image.
A first 3×3 convolution sees a small patch, while later stacked layers can respond to a wider area.
A detector needs enough receptive field to recognize a whole car rather than just one wheel.
A large theoretical field does not guarantee every input pixel has equal influence.
Insert gaps between kernel positions to expand the receptive field.
A filter can see farther without a proportional rise in weight count.
A 3×3 kernel with dilation 2 samples positions spaced two pixels apart.
A segmentation model uses dilated filters to gather context while keeping a fine output grid.
Large dilation can skip local details and create gridding artifacts.
Filter each input channel separately, then mix channels with 1×1 filters.
Separating spatial filtering from channel mixing can cut computation.
A mobile vision model applies one spatial filter per color-feature channel, then combines channels.
Compared with a full convolution, this design often uses fewer multiplications at similar feature-map size.
Lower cost may come with a quality trade-off; compare on the target device and task.
A 1×1 convolution that mixes channels at each spatial position.
It changes channel combinations without looking across neighboring pixels by itself.
At one pixel, a 1×1 layer combines 64 input channels into 32 output channels.
A depthwise-separable block uses pointwise convolution after per-channel spatial filtering.
A 1×1 filter alone cannot capture a new spatial pattern across nearby pixels.
A learned operation that increases the spatial size of a feature map.
It is commonly used in decoder paths to produce denser image outputs.
A segmentation decoder upsamples a 16×16 feature map toward a 32×32 map.
A generator expands a compact latent representation into a larger image grid.
Stride and padding choices can create checkerboard artifacts; inspect outputs.
Find and classify objects while estimating where they are in an image.
The output includes locations such as bounding boxes as well as class labels.
A traffic camera marks each visible car with a rectangle and a car score.
A wildlife model locates two birds in one photo rather than giving one whole-image label.
Detection quality depends on both the class and box placement.
Remove overlapping detection boxes that likely describe the same object.
Keep a high-scoring box and discard lower-scoring boxes with too much overlap.
A detector draws five boxes around one dog; NMS keeps the best box.
Two nearby people should keep separate boxes when their overlap is below the chosen cutoff.
An aggressive overlap threshold can wrongly remove real adjacent objects.
Measure overlap between two regions as intersection area divided by union area.
IoU is 1 for identical boxes and 0 when they do not overlap.
Two boxes overlap over 40 pixels and cover 100 pixels together, so IoU is 0.4.
A predicted box with IoU 0.8 against the true box is better aligned than one with IoU 0.2.
IoU measures location overlap, not whether the predicted class is correct.
Assign a class label to every image pixel.
The model colors regions by category rather than producing one label per image.
In a road scene, each pixel becomes road, vehicle, person, sky, or background.
A medical image can mark all pixels belonging to a tumor region.
Semantic segmentation does not distinguish two separate objects of the same class.
Predict a label for an entire image.
The output describes the whole image rather than each object’s location.
A model labels a photo as cat after seeing the full image.
A quality-control model labels a manufactured part as damaged or intact.
A single whole-image label can miss multiple objects or small important regions.
Use these concepts when building sequence models and language generators.
Run several attention operations in parallel and combine their outputs.
Different heads can learn different relationships in the same sequence.
One head may focus on a pronoun’s noun while another focuses on nearby word order.
A Transformer combines outputs from eight attention heads into one representation.
More heads do not guarantee more useful patterns; measure quality and compute cost.
Let one sequence attend to information from another sequence.
Queries come from one source while keys and values come from another.
A translation decoder looks at encoded source words while writing the next target word.
A text-to-image model lets image features attend to the user’s prompt.
Cross-attention differs from self-attention, where both sides come from the same sequence.
Block attention to future tokens during left-to-right generation.
At position t, the model can use earlier tokens but not tokens that come afterward.
While predicting the third word, a language model can read words one and two but not word four.
A triangular mask prevents a training example from revealing its next-token answer.
A causal mask is different from padding masks that hide empty positions.
Encode an input and then produce an output conditioned on that representation.
The encoder reads the source; the decoder generates the target.
A translation model encodes an English sentence and decodes a French one.
An image-captioning model encodes visual features and decodes a sentence.
Not every Transformer uses both halves; some models are encoder-only or decoder-only.
Train a model to recover hidden tokens from surrounding context.
The model can look both left and right of a hidden position.
Given “The cat sat on the [MASK],” the model predicts a likely missing word such as mat.
A text encoder learns representations by solving many masked-word tasks.
This objective differs from next-token generation and may need adaptation for generation.
Predict each next item using only earlier items in a sequence.
Generation repeats one next-step prediction at a time.
A language model predicts the next word after “The sky is,” then continues from its own output.
An image model can generate pixels or patches in a fixed order based on previous ones.
Errors can compound because later predictions depend on earlier generated choices.
Train a sequence decoder using the true previous token as its next input.
Correct history makes training easier, but inference uses the model’s own earlier outputs.
During training, a translator receives the correct prior French word before predicting the next.
At deployment, it must use the word it actually generated, even if that word was wrong.
The training–inference mismatch can cause errors to compound.
Keep several promising partial sequences while generating an answer.
At each step, expand candidates and retain the highest-scoring few.
A translator keeps its best four partial sentences instead of committing to only one word path.
Speech recognition compares several possible transcriptions before choosing a final sentence.
A wider beam can improve search yet still prefer short or repetitive outputs without scoring care.
Sample the next token from only the k highest-scoring candidates.
Discard lower-ranked tokens, renormalize the rest, and draw one.
With k = 3, a model chooses among only its top three next-word options.
Lower k makes text more predictable, while higher k allows more variety.
A fixed k ignores how concentrated or flat the probability distribution is.
Sample from the smallest next-token set whose probabilities reach a chosen total p.
The number of allowed tokens changes with the model’s uncertainty.
With p = 0.9, a confident step may allow two words while an uncertain step allows ten.
A writing assistant samples from the high-probability mass to balance coherence and variety.
A very low p can become repetitive; a very high p can admit unlikely words.
Use these ideas when generating data or adapting pretrained networks.
Learn a probabilistic latent representation and decode samples from it.
The encoder predicts a distribution, so nearby latent points can decode into related outputs.
A VAE trained on handwritten digits samples a latent point and generates a new digit image.
Interpolating between two encoded faces can produce a gradual transition in facial features.
A smooth latent space does not guarantee sharp or realistic generated images.
A learned coordinate space that represents useful hidden factors in data.
Similar inputs often occupy nearby regions in a useful learned representation.
A face model maps two photos of the same person to nearby feature vectors.
Moving along one learned direction in a generator may alter lighting while preserving identity.
Latent coordinates are model-dependent and do not always have a simple human meaning.
Generate data by learning to reverse a gradual noising process.
A denoising model repeatedly turns noisy input toward a plausible sample.
An image generator starts with random noise and removes noise over many steps to form a landscape.
A restoration model uses the same idea to recover a cleaner image from a damaged photo.
Sampling may require many steps, and the output still needs quality and safety evaluation.
Represent model weights or activations with fewer bits.
Smaller numeric formats can reduce model size and sometimes speed inference.
An eight-bit copy of a classifier uses less memory than its original 32-bit weights.
A phone runs a quantized speech model locally where the full-precision model would not fit.
Lower precision can reduce accuracy, especially for sensitive layers or extreme values.
Train a generator against a discriminator that tries to detect generated samples.
The two networks provide competing feedback during training.
A generator makes synthetic shoe images while a discriminator judges whether each looks real.
As both models improve, generated textures can become more convincing.
GAN training can be unstable or collapse to a narrow set of outputs.
A network trained to distinguish real data from generated data in a GAN.
Its feedback gives the generator a learning signal about plausibility.
A discriminator scores whether a face image came from the photo collection or the generator.
If generated shoes have unrealistic edges, its scores can push the generator to improve them.
An overly strong discriminator can leave the generator with weak training feedback.
Train a smaller student model to imitate a larger teacher model.
Soft teacher predictions can teach more than hard class labels alone.
A compact image classifier learns from a large model’s probabilities across animal classes.
A mobile chatbot student mimics a larger model so responses run faster on a device.
The student can inherit the teacher’s errors and may not match its full capability.
Adapt a frozen model using small trainable low-rank weight updates.
Most original weights stay fixed while a small set of added parameters learns the task.
A language model is adapted to legal summaries by training small matrices in selected layers.
Two adapters can customize the same base model for different writing styles.
A small adapter still needs representative data and may not solve a large domain gap.
Retrieve relevant external information before generating an answer.
The generator conditions its answer on fetched passages rather than only stored parameters.
A support assistant searches product manuals and cites the sections used in its reply.
A research helper retrieves recent internal notes before summarizing a project decision.
Retrieved documents can be irrelevant or wrong; verify sources and generated claims.
Store and search embeddings by similarity.
Nearby vectors can identify semantically related items for retrieval.
A question embedding finds similar manual passages even when the exact words differ.
An image search system retrieves product photos whose feature vectors resemble a query photo.
Similarity does not establish factual correctness; filtering and source checks still matter.
Use these terms when representing and evaluating language data.
Weight a word by its frequency in a document and its rarity across documents.
Common words receive less weight than terms that distinguish a particular document.
The word “volcano” gets a high weight in a geology article if it appears often there but rarely elsewhere.
A search engine ranks a document with specific query terms above one containing only common words.
TF-IDF ignores word order and does not understand meaning by itself.
Represent text using word counts without preserving word order.
Each document becomes a vector with one count per vocabulary term.
“Cats chase mice” becomes counts for cats, chase, and mice.
A spam filter learns from counts of words such as “offer” and “free” across messages.
“Dog bites person” and “person bites dog” can have identical counts despite different meanings.
A consecutive sequence of n tokens in text.
Groups of nearby tokens preserve limited local order.
The bigrams in “machine learning works” are “machine learning” and “learning works”.
A language model estimates how likely “New York” is from observed two-word sequences.
Large n-grams become sparse because many possible sequences rarely occur.
Identify text spans that name people, places, organizations, and similar entities.
The model labels which words refer to which entity types.
In “Ada visited London,” NER marks Ada as a person and London as a place.
A news tool extracts company and location names from thousands of articles.
Ambiguous names and new entities can be mislabeled without context.
Measure how surprised a language model is by a sequence of tokens.
Lower perplexity on the same evaluation set usually means better next-token prediction.
A model that assigns high probability to every word in a held-out sentence gets lower perplexity.
Two language models can be compared on the same tokenized test collection.
Perplexity values are not directly comparable across different tokenizers or datasets.
Compare generated text with reference text using matching word sequences.
It rewards overlap of short token sequences and penalizes very short output.
A machine translation shares many phrase sequences with a reference translation and scores higher.
Two valid translations with different wording may have low overlap despite both being good.
BLEU is a limited proxy for meaning and should not replace human evaluation.
Use these concepts when forecasting observations that arrive over time.
Measure how a series relates to shifted copies of itself.
Repeated patterns appear as strong relationships at particular time lags.
Daily electricity use may correlate with values seven days earlier because weekdays repeat.
An analyst checks lag-one autocorrelation to see whether yesterday’s value helps predict today’s.
A trend can create apparent correlation; inspect stationarity and seasonality.
A property where a time series has stable statistical behavior over time.
Roughly stable mean and variance make some forecasting methods easier to apply.
A sensor fluctuates around the same level for months without a lasting upward trend.
Differencing a steadily rising sales series can make its changes more stable.
Real data may change regime, so stationarity is an assumption to check rather than presume.
How far into the future a forecast predicts.
Longer horizons often carry more uncertainty and may require different features.
A power forecast predicts demand for the next hour, while another predicts the next seven days.
A retailer evaluates one-week and three-month forecasts separately because their uses differ.
Do not evaluate a long-horizon task using only one-step-ahead errors.
A recurring pattern at a regular time interval.
The pattern repeats by hour, week, month, year, or another cycle.
Ice-cream sales rise each summer and fall each winter.
A call center sees a similar workload spike every Monday morning.
Seasonality can change over time; a past cycle may not repeat exactly.
Use these ideas when an agent learns actions from rewards over time.
A framework with states, actions, transitions, rewards, and a policy.
The next outcome depends on the current state and action under the Markov assumption.
A robot state records its location; moving right may reach a new square and earn a reward.
A delivery agent chooses routes while balancing travel time and future opportunities.
An incomplete state can violate the Markov assumption by hiding important history.
A rule or probability distribution that chooses an action from a state.
A policy describes the agent’s behavior at each decision point.
A gridworld policy says move right from the start square and up near the goal.
A game agent chooses an action with probabilities that change as its strategy improves.
A high reward in training does not guarantee the policy is safe in a new environment.
Expected future return from a state when following a policy.
It summarizes how promising a state is under the chosen behavior.
A square near a goal can have high value if the policy usually reaches the goal from there.
A game agent estimates that a losing board position has a low expected future return.
Value depends on the policy and reward definition, not only the visible state.
Expected future return after taking action a in state s and following a policy afterward.
It compares available actions within the same state.
At an intersection, going left has Q = 4 while going right has Q = 7, so right looks better.
A learner updates the Q value of a move after observing its reward and next state.
Q values depend on the reward scale and the policy used after the first action.
Express a value as immediate reward plus discounted future value.
A long decision problem becomes a relationship between neighboring states.
A route worth 2 now plus 0.9 times a next-state value of 5 has target value 6.5.
A value-iteration step updates each grid cell from its possible successors.
An incorrect transition model or discount factor can produce misleading values.
Choose a random action with probability epsilon and a best-known action otherwise.
Occasional exploration helps discover actions the current policy may miss.
With epsilon 0.1, a robot tries a random move about one time in ten.
An agent gradually lowers epsilon as it learns which routes usually pay off.
Exploration can be costly or unsafe when actions affect real systems.
Store past transitions and sample them later for learning.
Reusing varied past experience can reduce correlation between consecutive updates.
A game agent records state, action, reward, and next state after every move.
A learner trains on a shuffled minibatch of old and recent transitions.
A replay buffer can overrepresent stale behavior if its contents are not managed.
A delayed copy of a value network used to calculate learning targets.
Slower target changes can stabilize bootstrapped updates.
A DQN updates its online network each step but copies weights to the target network only periodically.
A target value for a saved transition comes from the slower-moving network.
A target network does not fix poor rewards or inadequate exploration.
Adjust policy parameters in a direction that raises expected reward.
The algorithm learns action probabilities directly rather than only estimating values.
A robot increases the probability of turns that led to successful deliveries.
A game agent uses sampled episodes to improve the probability of winning moves.
Gradient estimates can be noisy and require enough experience for stable learning.
Combine a policy learner (actor) with a value estimator (critic).
The critic evaluates outcomes and helps guide actor updates.
An actor chooses a robot movement while the critic estimates whether it improved future return.
A game learner updates both its action policy and its state-value estimate after a round.
A poor critic can send misleading feedback to the actor.
Use these ideas when reasoning about search, decisions, and symbolic AI.
Explore possible states and actions to find a path to a goal.
Each node is a state and each edge represents an available action.
A maze solver expands reachable rooms until it finds the exit.
A puzzle solver explores legal tile moves to reach the target arrangement.
The number of states may grow rapidly, so search strategy and pruning matter.
A search estimate that never exceeds the true cheapest cost to a goal.
For A* with suitable assumptions, underestimation supports optimal path finding.
Straight-line distance is a lower bound on road distance when routes cannot be shorter than the line.
A puzzle heuristic counts tiles out of place without claiming extra moves that are not required.
A heuristic that overestimates may cause A* to miss the least-cost path.
Expand paths using cost so far plus an estimated remaining cost.
The priority score f(n) = g(n) + h(n) balances progress made with estimated distance left.
A map planner picks a road junction with low travel cost plus low estimated distance to the destination.
A tile-puzzle solver prioritizes boards with few moves used and a small remaining-distance estimate.
Optimality depends on the heuristic and search conditions; a bad estimate can mislead search.
Choose moves by assuming an opponent will choose the strongest reply.
The maximizing player prefers the move with the best worst-case outcome.
A tic-tac-toe player compares moves after considering the opponent’s best response.
A chess agent searches a limited game tree and evaluates leaf positions.
Full trees grow exponentially, so practical play needs depth limits or pruning.
Skip minimax branches that cannot affect the final decision.
Bounds on the best alternatives allow some game-tree paths to be ignored.
After finding a strong winning move, a chess search skips a reply branch that is already worse.
Good move ordering lets alpha–beta examine fewer nodes before choosing the same move.
It speeds exact minimax search but does not improve a weak evaluation function.
Choose variable values that satisfy a set of constraints.
Search can reject partial assignments as soon as they violate a rule.
Sudoku assigns digits to squares while keeping each row, column, and box valid.
A timetable assigns classes to rooms without overlapping teachers or room bookings.
A valid solution may still be undesirable unless preferences are modeled separately.
Represent entities and relationships as connected nodes and edges.
Explicit links let systems query how facts relate.
A graph connects a medicine to its active ingredient and the conditions it treats.
A recommendation service links authors, books, topics, and reader interests.
Incorrect or outdated edges can propagate misleading answers.
Use encoded domain rules and facts to make recommendations or deductions.
Its decisions follow explicit rules supplied by people or knowledge sources.
A troubleshooting tool asks about symptoms and follows rules to suggest a likely hardware fault.
A tax helper applies a documented set of eligibility rules to a user’s answers.
Rules require maintenance and may fail on cases outside the encoded knowledge.
Grow a decision tree using repeated simulated play and outcome estimates.
The search balances trying promising moves with exploring less-tested moves.
A Go program simulates continuations from candidate moves and spends more trials on useful branches.
A planning agent runs rollouts before choosing between possible next actions.
Results depend on simulation quality and available computation.
The number of future steps considered in a decision plan.
A longer horizon can account for delayed effects but costs more computation.
A robot plans three moves ahead to avoid a nearby wall.
An energy controller plans a day ahead to use cheap electricity overnight.
A short horizon may miss delayed rewards; a long horizon can magnify model errors.
Add the input back to the layer’s output so a deep stack can still learn “do nothing.”
A staircase with a slide beside it. If the stairs are useless, you can still slide down the original path.
Deep nets die when every layer must rewrite the signal. A residual says: keep the old story, plus a small edit.
A plain layer computes F(x). A residual block computes x + F(x). The extra x is the skip (or shortcut) connection.
If the best edit is “nothing,” F can learn zeros and the signal still arrives. That is why 50-layer ResNets train when 50 plain layers would not.
The skip also gives gradients a highway. Blame can jump over a bad layer instead of vanishing in a long product.
output = original input plus whatever this block wants to add
x = [1, 2]. The block wants to add [0.1, −0.2].
y = [1.1, 1.8]. The original 1 and 2 are still mostly there.
If F were [0, 0], y would equal x. The “do nothing” door stays open.
A residual is an edit, not a rewrite.
In the demo, turn the skip off and watch the signal fade across layers.
Set the block to zeros and confirm the output still equals the input.
Deep CNNs, Transformers, and any stack where you want identity as an easy option.
Shapes must match to add. If F changes width, project x with a 1×1 conv or a linear layer first.
Each word asks: who should I look at? Then it mixes those voices by importance.
In a noisy room you turn toward the person who said your name. Attention is that head-turn, written as numbers.
A sentence is not a blender. “Not good” needs “not” to look at “good,” not at a random earlier word.
Query is the question (“who matters to me?”). Keys are name-tags. Values are what those people actually said.
Score = Query · Key. Softmax turns scores into shares that add to 100%. The output is a weighted mix of values.
Self-attention means every token asks every other token in the same sentence. Multi-head attention asks the same question in several accents (syntax, names, negation).
compare questions to name-tags, turn the scores into shares, then mix what was said
The query for “not” scores 2.0 with “good”, 0.2 with “very”, 0.1 with itself.
Softmax of those scores (T=1) puts most mass on “good.”
The mixed value is mostly the “good” vector, a little of the others.
The model can now represent “not-good” instead of averaging the whole sentence.
Attention is a soft lookup, not a blender.
In the demo, raise one key’s match and watch that token’s share grow.
Raise temperature and watch the shares flatten toward “everyone equally.”
Transformers, machine translation, any sequence where “who refers to whom” matters.
Cost grows with sequence length squared. Also, attention is not understanding — it is a weighted mix.
Turn a name or token into a short list of learned numbers that sit near similar names.
A seating chart. “King” and “queen” sit at nearby tables. “Banana” sits in another room.
One-hot is honest but lonely: every name is equally far. An embedding lets the model invent a map.
An embedding table has one row per token. Looking up “cat” returns, say, 32 numbers. Those numbers start random and become meaning.
Nearby vectors mean “used in similar ways.” King − man + woman ≈ queen is the famous cartoon of that geometry.
We use embeddings for words, users, movies, and high-cardinality cities — anywhere one-hot would be a mile wide.
the embedding of token i is just row i of a learned table
Cat and dog are close. Car is far.
A linear layer can now treat “animal-ish” as a direction.
Training nudges the points until neighbors match the task.
An embedding is a learned address, not a definition in English.
In the demo, drag two words together and watch cosine rise.
Compare one-hot (all far) with the embedding map (some near).
NLP, recommenders, and any categorical feature with too many unique values for one-hot.
Rare tokens stay noisy. Out-of-vocabulary words need an UNK row. Do not treat the axes as human-named traits unless you checked.
A softness knob on softmax: low T is a confident peak, high T is a flatter share-out.
A spicy debate vs a polite round-table. Low temperature picks a winner. High temperature lets everyone talk.
The same three scores can look like 95% sure or like a shrug — temperature is that mood.
Softmax uses exp(score / T). Divide by a small T and the biggest score explodes relative to the others.
T → 0 is almost argmax (one-hot). T → ∞ is almost uniform (everyone gets 1/n).
People use temperature in sampling (chatty vs greedy text) and in distillation (a teacher speaks softly so a student can copy the whole ranking).
divide the scores by T before you turn them into shares
T = 0.4: the leader takes almost all of it.
T = 3: the bars flatten toward even thirds.
Temperature does not change who is ahead. It changes how loudly we announce it.
On the softmax demo, drag T and watch the bars.
Say out loud: “same ranking, different confidence.”
Sampling from language models, knowledge distillation, and anytime softmax feels too peaky or too mushy.
T is not a learning rate. Also, T ≤ 0 is undefined. Calibration is a different job than “make it spicier.”
A plot of train vs validation error as you add data or training time.
A report card over the semester — not one quiz, the whole trend.
One score is a snapshot. A learning curve tells you whether more data, more time, or a different family is the medicine.
Two common x-axes: number of training examples, or epoch. Y is error (or the opposite: accuracy).
If train is great and val is stuck high, you are overfitting — more data or more seatbelts. If both are high, you are underfitting — richer model or better features.
A gap that never closes even with more data often means the family is wrong, not that you need one more epoch.
how the two errors move as the homework pile or the semester grows
You plot val error against dataset size.
Both curves high and flat: underfit. A line cannot learn a bowl.
Train low, val high, gap stays: overfit. Collect more rows or regularize.
Both falling toward the same floor: you are in the healthy middle.
Read the pair of curves, not a single trophy number.
In the demo, switch the story (under / over / healthy) and name the medicine.
Open a lab and watch the live train/val lines — that is this term.
Every training run. Also when someone asks “should we label 10,000 more rows?”
A tiny val set makes a jumpy curve. Smooth with a moving average or more folds before you panic.
The boring guess you must beat before you celebrate a fancy model.
Before you praise a weather app, check “tomorrow will be like today.” If the app loses to that, it is not clever.
A neural net that is worse than “always predict the mean” is a costume, not a win.
Regression baseline: predict the training mean (or median). Classification: predict the majority class. Forecasting: persist the last value.
A slightly less boring baseline is a linear model or a shallow tree. Fancy models should beat both.
Report the baseline next to your score. “92% accuracy” is a shrug if 91% of rows are the same class.
the simplest honest guess — often the average or the most common label
A mailbox that is almost all ham.
A net that says “ham” always also scores 95%.
You need precision/recall on spam, or a model that beats 95% for a reason.
Always write the boring number first.
In the demo, change the class balance and watch the majority score move.
Before any lab run, ask: what is the mean / majority here?
The first hour of every project, and every slide that shows a metric.
A leaked feature can beat the baseline for a dishonest reason. Also pick a metric that matches the job, not just accuracy.
The answer (or a peek at the future) sneaks into the homework.
Studying with the sealed exam already in the backpack. The score is a confession.
Magical validation scores that die in production are usually leakage, not genius.
Target leakage: a column that is the label in disguise (or decided after the label). “Paid_off” predicting “will default.”
Split leakage: you scale, impute, or augment using test rows, or the same patient sits in train and test.
Time leakage: tomorrow’s weather trains yesterday’s model. Shuffle is the usual villain in forecasts.
\text{if } x \text{ knows } y \text{ too early, the score is fake}
if a feature could not exist at prediction time, it is a cheat
A patient appears in both train and test with a unique hospital style.
The model memorizes the hospital, not the disease.
A new hospital arrives. The magic vanishes.
Split by the real unit: patient, household, day — not by row if rows are twins.
In the demo, leak the label into a feature and watch the score jump.
Ask of every column: “would I have this at 9am on prediction day?”
Every dataset review, especially medical, finance, and time series.
Preprocessing fit on all data. Group twins. Target-derived features. “Future” timestamps.
How aligned two arrows are, ignoring how long they are.
Two flashlights. Cosine asks whether they point the same way, not how bright they are.
A long review and a short review can mean the same thing. Cosine ignores the shout and keeps the direction.
Cosine is the dot product after both vectors are stretched to length 1. Range is −1 (opposite) to 1 (same way). 0 is sideways.
That is why search and embeddings love it: document length should not win the race.
If you already L2-normalized the rows, cosine and dot product are the same number.
agreeing pairs, divided by each arrow’s length
Same direction-ish, not twins. Scale b to [10, 10] and cosine stays 0.71.
Length dropped out. Only the angle stayed.
In the demo, stretch one vector without turning it. Cosine should hold still.
Turn it 90° and watch cosine fall to 0.
Embeddings, retrieval, recommenders, any “are these about the same thing?”
Uncentered counts can make everything look similar. Also, cosine 0.99 is not a proof of meaning — check the task.
Fill the edges so every example (or every convolution) has the same shape.
A photo in a frame. You add a white border so a stack of photos is the same size, or so the filter can sit on the corners.
Batches and convolutions are picky about shape. Padding is the honest filler — usually zeros, sometimes a special PAD token.
Sequence padding: short sentences get PAD tokens on the end (or the start) so a batch is a rectangle. The model must learn to ignore PAD.
Convolution padding: extra zeros around an image so the output stays the same height/width (“same” padding). “Valid” means no pad, so the picture shrinks.
Masking tells attention “this slot is fake.” Without a mask, PAD can steal attention mass.
glue empty slots on the end (or the border) until the shape matches
The loss and attention should skip those PADs.
Padding is shape, not meaning. Mask it.
In the demo, shorten a sentence and watch PAD tiles appear.
Toggle a mask and see whether PAD still gets a share.
Any batched sequence model, and CNNs when you want “same” spatial size.
Right vs left pad can change RNNs. Too much pad wastes compute. Never treat PAD as a real word in metrics.
The atom a language model actually sees: a word, a piece of a word, or a special mark.
Lego bricks. “unbelievable” might be three bricks: un + believe + able. The model builds with bricks, not with English essays.
A model does not read letters the way you do. It reads a list of IDs. Each ID is a token.
Whitespace split is the old toy. Modern models use subwords (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece) so rare words still share pieces.
Special tokens mark the start, the pad, the unknown, or the end. They are just more IDs in the table.
Context length is counted in tokens, not words. A long word can be many tokens and cost more.
cut text into pieces, then replace each piece with its ID in the vocabulary
A word tokenizer might give [The, cats, sat, .].
A subword tokenizer might give [The, cat, s, sat, .].
Each piece becomes an ID, then an embedding row.
Token first, embedding second, attention third.
In the demo, type a word and watch it split into pieces.
Count tokens, not words, when you talk about context length.
Every NLP pipeline. Also when you budget API cost or context windows.
Different tokenizers split the same sentence differently. Compare token counts, not word counts. Leading spaces are often part of the token.
Move one control and say what changed in one sentence.
Keep this page small: one idea, one picture.
The curve or plane that separates predicted classes in feature space.
On one side of the boundary the model says class A; on the other, class B.
Linear models draw a straight cut. Nearest-neighbor paints regions around training points.
The boundary is the set of points the model scores as a tie.
A table of actual class versus predicted class: TP, FP, FN, TN.
Rows are the true labels; columns are what the model predicted.
Every common binary metric is a ratio of these four cells.
Accuracy is correct cells over all cells.
A plot of true-positive rate versus false-positive rate as the threshold moves.
Each threshold is one point (FPR, TPR). Sweeping the threshold traces the curve.
AUC is the area under that curve. ROC is not the right summary for every problem — especially heavy class imbalance, prefer PR curves.
TPR is recall; FPR is the false-alarm rate among actual negatives.
Precision: of predicted positives, how many were right. Recall: of actual positives, how many were found.
Precision cares about false alarms. Recall cares about misses.
You usually cannot max both without changing the threshold or the model.
Precision uses the predicted-positive column; recall uses the actual-positive row.
The harmonic mean of precision and recall — low if either one is low.
F1 is not the ordinary average. A 0.9 / 0.2 pair does not score “pretty good”.
Use it when you care about the positive class and want one number.
Harmonic mean of precision P and recall R.
Correct predictions divided by all predictions.
On 95 negatives and 5 positives, “always negative” scores 95% and still misses every rare event.
Share of predictions that match the true label.
Do not lead with accuracy on imbalanced labels.
When one class is much rarer than another, accuracy can look fine while the rare class is ignored.
Dummy majority classifiers set a high accuracy floor.
Typical responses: class weights, resampling, and metrics such as recall or PR-AUC. None is universally best.
Increase the minority class by repeating or synthesizing examples.
Duplicates do not add new information.
SMOTE synthesizes points between neighbors instead of copying.
Reduce the majority class so class counts are closer.
You throw away majority rows. That can help or hurt depending on how unique those rows were.
Synthetic minority points placed on the line between a point and a neighbor.
Not a copy. An interpolation. Still not real new measurements.
Compute similarity in a richer feature space without building that space.
A conceptual map φ can make a curved 2D pattern linearly separable.
A kernel K(x, x′) = φ(x)·φ(x′) skips constructing φ. The lift picture is conceptual, not stored coordinates.
The kernel is the inner product after a feature map, computed directly.
A training point that sits on the margin and pins the SVM boundary.
Move a support vector and the boundary moves. Interior points usually do not.
The gap between the decision boundary and the nearest support vectors.
Hard margin: no points inside the gap.
Soft margin (C): some slack is allowed so outliers do not dictate the plane.
How mixed a node’s class labels are. Pure nodes have entropy near 0.
A 50/50 split is the noisiest binary node. Trees split to drop entropy.
Minus the sum of p log p over classes.
Another mix score: 1 minus the sum of squared class shares.
Same story as entropy, slightly different curve. CART often uses Gini because it is cheap.
Zero when one class has share 1.
How much impurity drops after a split, weighted by child sizes.
IG = impurity(parent) − weighted impurity(children). Trees pick the split with the largest gain.
Parent entropy minus the size-weighted child entropies.
Remove extra branches so a tree is smaller and often generalizes better.
Deep trees memorize. Cost-complexity pruning collapses twigs that buy little impurity drop.
Sample the same size as the dataset, with replacement. Repeats and omissions are expected.
Ordinary sampling without replacement never repeats. Bootstrap does.
Train models on bootstrap samples in parallel, then vote or average.
Parallel, not sequential. Classification votes; regression averages. Random Forest is bagged trees.
Add models one after another; each focuses on leftover errors.
Sequential, not parallel. AdaBoost reweights examples; gradient boosting fits residuals.
A model-specific ranking of which inputs it used. Not a causal claim.
Tree importance, permutation importance, and coefficients disagree. Treat ranks as “this model leaned on…”. The bars here are illustrative.
Local explanation: base value plus feature contributions ≈ this prediction.
Waterfall charts add signed contributions onto a baseline.
This studio shows the shape of the idea. Bars are illustrative, not computed Shapley values.
Map each category to an integer code. The number is not an order unless the category truly is ordered.
Red=0, Blue=1 does not mean Blue > Red. Use one-hot when the model would treat codes as distances.
Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation. Mean ≈ 0, SD ≈ 1.
Does not make data Gaussian. It only rescales. Fit mean/SD on train, apply to val/test.
z-score: centered and scaled by training SD.
Linearly map a feature from its min–max range onto [0, 1].
Different from vector (L2) normalization, which rescales a whole vector to length 1.
Sensitive to extreme min/max. Fit on train only.
Shift by min, divide by the range.
Sensitive to feature scale — hence scaling before k-NN or k-means.
City-block distance: add absolute gaps. No diagonal shortcut.
Measure the gap along each feature separately, then add those gaps.
It is often useful when movement or differences are naturally measured one coordinate at a time.
Slide a small kernel, multiply overlapping cells, sum — that sum is one feature-map cell.
The same small set of filter weights is reused at every location.
This lets a CNN recognize a local pattern wherever it appears in an image.
The small grid of weights that convolution slides. Edge, blur, and sharpen are classic hand-made kernels.
CNNs learn these weights. Presets here are teaching examples, not a trained net.
How many cells the convolution window jumps. Stride 2 halves spatial size.
A smaller stride checks more neighboring positions and usually gives a larger output grid.
A larger stride skips positions, reducing computation and spatial detail.
Extra border cells (often zeros) so the window can sit on the edge. Valid = no pad; same ≈ keep size.
Different from NLP padding, which fills token sequences to a common length.
Downsample a feature map: max or average over small windows.
Max pooling keeps the strongest response in each window; average pooling keeps their mean.
The smaller output helps the network focus on prominent patterns while using less computation.
The grid of filter responses after convolution — where the kernel “fired”.
Each cell records how strongly one filter matched a particular location.
Different filters produce different maps, such as one highlighting edges and another highlighting textures.
A network that steps through a sequence, carrying a hidden state from t to t+1.
At each step, the model combines the new input with its memory of earlier inputs.
That memory can help with ordered data such as words or measurements over time, though basic RNNs struggle with very long gaps.
A recurrent cell with forget, input, and output gates plus a cell state that can carry memory farther.
Forget how much old cell to keep. Input how much new candidate to write. Output how much cell to emit as hidden.
Tokens in the same sequence attend to each other. Click one token to see the mix.
Each token assigns weights to other tokens and combines their information.
The weights can highlight relevant context, but a large attention weight alone is not a full explanation of a prediction.
Query: what am I looking for? Key: what do I contain? Value: what information do I provide?
A query is compared with keys to score which positions matter.
Those scores weight the corresponding values, producing a context-aware representation.
A tag for token order. Attention alone has no inherent left-to-right.
Position information is added to token representations so the model can distinguish different orders.
The position signal may be fixed by a formula or learned from training data.
Reuse a pretrained backbone, then adapt a head to a new task.
A model trained on a large source task has already learned useful general patterns.
Reusing those patterns can reduce the data and training time needed for a related task.
Unfreeze some or all pretrained layers and keep training on the target task.
Feature extraction freezes the backbone. Fine-tuning updates it. Not a second full Transfer Learning lesson.
Weights scale each input. Bias shifts the firing threshold.
A neuron adds the weighted inputs and the bias before applying its activation.

Depth-Limited Search (DLS) follows depth-first traversal to a fixed depth ℓ. A goal test comes before the cutoff test. CUTOFF means a deeper search may help; FAILURE means the explored subtree is exhausted. It uses memory proportional to the active path and its pending successors.

DLS(node, goal, remaining):
  if node == goal: return SUCCESS
  if remaining == 0: return CUTOFF
  cutoff_occurred = false
  for child in successors(node):
    result = DLS(child, goal, remaining - 1)
    if result == SUCCESS: return SUCCESS
    if result == CUTOFF: cutoff_occurred = true
  if cutoff_occurred: return CUTOFF
  return FAILURE
A larger depth limit may help
The depth bound stopped exploration; the algorithm has not ruled out deeper solutions.

IDA* runs depth-first contours under f(n)=g(n)+h(n). Each unsuccessful pass returns the smallest f-value that exceeded the bound. With an admissible heuristic and positive costs, the first solution is optimal. This grid uses four-way unit-cost motion and Manhattan distance.

IDA_STAR(start, goal):
  bound = h(start)
  while true:
    t = contour(start, 0, bound)
    if t == FOUND: return path
    if t == infinity: return FAILURE
    bound = t  # minimum exceeded f

contour(node, g, bound):
  f = g + h(node)
  if f > bound: return f
  if node == goal: return FOUND
  minimum = infinity
  for child not on current path:
    t = contour(child, g + cost, bound)
    if t == FOUND: return FOUND
    minimum = min(minimum, t)
  return minimum
How is the next contour bound chosen?
Minimum f that exceeded the previous bound
The returned minimum exceeded f avoids skipping a potentially optimal contour.

RBFS explores the most promising successor while retaining alternative backed-up f-costs. Successor f is max(g+h, parent f). Recursion is bounded by the minimum of the current limit and the next-best alternative. A failed branch returns an updated bound, allowing the search to switch branches.

RBFS(node, g, limit):
  if goal(node): return SUCCESS, node.f
  successors = expand(node)
  if empty(successors): return FAILURE, infinity
  for s in successors:
    s.f = max(g + cost(node,s) + h(s), node.f)
  while true:
    best = lowest_f(successors)
    alternative = second_lowest_f(successors)
    if best.f > limit: return FAILURE, best.f
    result, best.f = RBFS(best, g + cost,
                          min(limit, alternative.f))
    if result == SUCCESS: return SUCCESS, best.f
Which bound is used for recursive expansion?
The alternative limits how much work RBFS should spend on its current best branch.

AO* searches a partial AND/OR solution graph. OR alternatives compete by minimum cost; an AND hyperedge requires all its children and sums their edge-plus-subproblem costs. Expand an unsolved leaf of the marked best partial solution, back up costs, and propagate solved flags. Zero initial estimates here are admissible.

AO_STAR(root):
  mark_best_partial_solution(root)
  while not solved(root):
    leaf = unsolved_marked_leaf(root)
    expand(leaf)
    for node in reverse_dependency_order:
      for hyperedge in alternatives(node):
        cost = sum(edge_cost + child.cost)
      node.cost = min(alternative_costs)
      mark minimum_cost hyperedge
      node.solved = all(marked_children.solved)
  return marked_solution_graph
When is an AND hyperedge solved?
An AND choice is a joint subproblem requiring all children.

Backtracking assigns one variable at a time and rejects values that violate a constraint with an assigned neighbor. MRV chooses the smallest current domain; degree breaks toward highly connected variables. Least-constraining-value ordering preserves options for neighbors. Exhausting a variable restores the preceding assignment.

BACKTRACK(assignment):
  if complete(assignment): return SUCCESS
  v = select_unassigned_variable()
  for value in ordered_domain(v):
    if consistent(v, value, assignment):
      assignment[v] = value
      if BACKTRACK(assignment): return SUCCESS
      remove assignment[v]
  return FAILURE
What must hold for a complete map coloring?
Every region has the same color
Every adjacent pair has different colors
Every variable must be assigned and every binary inequality constraint satisfied.

Forward checking removes an assigned value from the domains of unassigned neighbors connected by inequality constraints. An empty domain causes immediate backtracking. A saved domain snapshot is restored when undoing an assignment. It is stronger than checking only already-assigned variables, but does not enforce all arc consistency.

FORWARD_CHECK(assignment, domains):
  if complete(assignment): return SUCCESS
  v = select_unassigned_variable()
  for value in ordered_domain(v):
    if consistent(v, value):
      saved = copy(domains)
      assignment[v] = value
      prune value from unassigned_neighbors(v)
      if no_empty_domain and recurse(): return SUCCESS
      domains = saved
      remove assignment[v]
  return FAILURE
What happens when a neighboring domain becomes empty?
No future assignment can repair the empty domain without undoing an earlier choice.

AC-3 maintains directed arcs (Xi,Xj). REVISE removes each value in Di that has no supporting value in Dj under the actual constraint. If Di changes, incoming arcs (Xk,Xi), excluding Xj, must be reconsidered. An empty domain proves inconsistency. Queue exhaustion proves arc consistency, not global satisfiability.

AC3(domains, constraints):
  Q = all_directed_arcs(constraints)
  while Q not empty:
    Xi, Xj = pop(Q)
    if REVISE(Xi, Xj):
      if empty(domain[Xi]): return FAILURE
      for Xk in neighbors(Xi) except Xj:
        enqueue(Q, (Xk, Xi))
  return SUCCESS

REVISE(Xi, Xj):
  remove x in Di if no y in Dj satisfies Cij(x,y)
  return whether Di changed
Does queue exhaustion guarantee a complete solution?
Local support on each binary arc need not imply a globally consistent complete assignment.

Min-conflicts starts with a complete N-Queens assignment, one queen per column. At each iteration choose a conflicted queen and move it to a row minimizing attacks with all other queens. Ties use seeded random choice. A step limit is inconclusive; restart changes the seed and initial board.

MIN_CONFLICTS(N, max_steps):
  board = random_complete_assignment(N)
  for step in range(max_steps):
    if no_conflicts(board): return SUCCESS
    column = random_conflicted_column(board)
    scores = conflicts_for_each_row(column)
    row = random_argmin(scores)
    board[column] = row
  return STEP_LIMIT
Does reaching the step limit prove N-Queens is impossible?
No; local search may be stuck
Min-conflicts is incomplete. A restart can escape an unproductive assignment.

Expectimax models actions with stochastic outcomes. MAX takes the highest successor value; CHANCE computes Σ p(outcome) × utility. Outgoing probabilities are normalized and nonnegative. Adjust the first-outcome probability to change both expectation calculations and the preferred action.
How does a chance node combine utilities?
Expected utility weights each outcome by its probability.

Exact Bayesian inference restricts factors to evidence, multiplies factors containing an elimination variable, then sums out that variable. Repeat until only the query remains and normalize. The burglary network uses standard binary CPTs; evidence J=true alone gives a much smaller posterior than the illustrative mockup number.

VARIABLE_ELIMINATION(query, evidence):
  factors = restrict_each_CPT(evidence)
  for variable in elimination_order:
    if variable in query or evidence: continue
    selected = factors_containing(variable)
    product = multiply(selected)
    reduced = sum_out(product, variable)
    replace selected with reduced
  result = multiply(factors)
  return normalize(result)
Does elimination order change the exact posterior?
No, but it changes intermediate factor sizes
Valid orders compute the same exact marginal; their time and memory costs can differ.

Sum-product alternates variable-to-factor products (excluding the recipient) and factor-to-variable sums over other variables. Messages and beliefs are normalized. On a tree the converged result is exact. On a loopy graph it is approximate, even when residuals converge. Damping retains a fraction of the previous message.

SUM_PRODUCT(factor_graph):
  initialize normalized messages
  repeat:
    for variable x and adjacent factor f:
      m_xf = local(x) * product(m_gx, g != f)
    for factor f and adjacent variable x:
      m_fx = sum_other_states(f * product(m_yf))
    normalize every message
    optionally damp with previous messages
    belief[x] = normalize(local(x) * product(m_fx))
    residual = max_absolute_message_change
    if residual < tolerance: stop
Are converged loopy beliefs necessarily exact?
Convergence alone does not remove the approximation introduced by loops.

Sequential Monte Carlo predicts particles using the motion model, multiplies old weights by observation likelihoods, normalizes, and estimates state with a weighted mean. ESS=1/Σw² measures degeneracy. Systematic resampling draws according to cumulative weight and resets all weights to 1/N.

PARTICLE_FILTER(particles, observation):
  predict each particle from motion_model
  weight *= observation_likelihood
  normalize weights using log-sum-exp
  estimate = sum(weight * state)
  ESS = 1 / sum(weight ** 2)
  if ESS < threshold * N:
    particles = systematic_resample(particles)
    weights = 1 / N
  return estimate
Few particles carry most of the probability mass, making resampling useful.

A probability distribution over hidden states

Model-free Monte Carlo control samples complete episodes from an ε-greedy policy. Discounted returns are computed backward after termination. First-visit updates only the earliest occurrence of each (s,a) within the episode; every-visit updates all occurrences. Incremental sample means estimate Q and improve the ε-greedy policy.

MONTE_CARLO_CONTROL():
  initialize Q and counts to zero
  for episode in episodes:
    trajectory = generate_complete_episode(epsilon_greedy(Q))
    G = 0
    compute all returns backward: G = reward + gamma * G
    for transition in chronological_order:
      if every_visit or first_occurrence(s,a):
        N[s,a] += 1
        Q[s,a] += (G[s,a] - Q[s,a]) / N[s,a]
    policy = epsilon_greedy(Q)
When does a Monte Carlo update use a return?
Monte Carlo uses complete sampled returns rather than bootstrapped Q targets.

DQN approximates four action values with a trainable 25→24→16→4 ReLU network. The online network receives minibatch gradients; a frozen target network supplies Bellman targets and synchronizes periodically. Uniform replay samples are drawn without replacement. The loss and reward curves come from actual training; short runs need not converge.

DQN():
  initialize online network and replay buffer
  target.copy_from(online)
  for environment step:
    action = epsilon_greedy(online(state))
    next_state, reward, done = environment.step(action)
    replay.add(state, action, reward, next_state, done)
    batch = uniform_sample_without_replacement(replay)
    y = reward if done else reward + gamma * max(target(next_state))
    loss = mean((online(state)[action] - y) ** 2)
    backpropagate loss through online network
    every C steps: target.copy_from(online)
The target stays frozen between explicit copies from the online network.

A small multilayer perceptron. Inputs are the features you enable (X₁, X₂, squares, product, sines). Hidden layers use tanh, ReLU, sigmoid, or linear. The last unit is a sigmoid, so the field is P(class 1).
Forward: z = W·h + b, then an activation. Loss: binary cross-entropy on a mini-batch. Backward: gradients flow to every weight. Update: Adam or SGD with optional L1 / L2. Play just repeats that step.

What changed from vanilla gradient descent?

SGD estimates the gradient from a noisy mini-batch. Momentum keeps a velocity term so updates continue in consistent directions. Adam keeps bias-corrected first and second moments, then scales the update by estimated gradient variance.
Vanilla GD is easiest to understand, SGD is useful for large datasets, Momentum helps with narrow valleys, and Adam is often a strong default when gradients vary widely by parameter.
